deep.reconstruction:
The page is a printed page from Christian Leiste's arithmetic and algebra textbook (bundle 'HB.Leiste'), p. 22. It has two short handwritten annotations, probably by Gauss. Part of the facing manuscript page is visible at the right edge.

Printed text:

(1) Closing sentence of §53: by dividing the exponent (logarithm) of a power by the root index, logarithms give roots of any order.

(2) §54 (Zusatz): rational exponents, for a>0.
- sqrt(a) = a^(1/2)
- cbrt(a^2) = a^(2/3)
- a*sqrt(a) = a^(1+1/2) = a^(3/2)
- 1/sqrt(a) = 1/a^(1/2) = a^(-1/2), citing §51 (a^(-n) = 1/a^n)
- a^2 / cbrt(a^4) = a^(2-4/3) = a^((6-4)/3) = a^(2/3) = cbrt(a^2)
- cbrt(a)*sqrt(a) = a^(1/3)*a^(1/2) = a^(1/3+1/2) = a^((2+3)/6) = (a^5)^(1/6)
- cbrt(a)/sqrt(a) = a^(1/3-1/2) = a^(-1/6) = 1/a^(1/6)
All of this can also be done with logarithms: log of the result = sum or difference of the exponents times log a.

(3) §55 (axioms): equal quantities raised to the same power, or with roots of the same degree extracted, give equal results. Their exponents and logarithms are then also equal.

(4) §56: from the sign rule §39a, (-a)(-a) = (+a)(+a) = a^2, so sqrt(a^2) = ±a. If ±c = a^m, then c^2 = a^(2m) is positive whichever sign c has. Hence every even power (handwritten insertion: 'als Producte aus ihren Wurzeln betrachtet', i.e. regarded as a product of its roots) of a real quantity is positive. A quantity -c^2 = -a^(2m) therefore cannot be such a square. So sqrt(-b), the root of a number thought of as a square yet negative (margin note: 'Wurzel aus einem negat. Quadrate'), is an 'impossible', 'imaginary' or 'imagined' quantity. If such quantities appear in a problem and cannot be eliminated, the problem contains something impossible. Hence one must learn to calculate with them.

(5) §57: sqrt(-a)*sqrt(-a) = -a (by the definition of the square root, §40). Hence, by division (§15), (-a)/sqrt(-a) = sqrt(-a). Special case: -1/sqrt(-1) = sqrt(-1), i.e. -1/i = i.

(6) §58: sqrt(+a)*sqrt(-b) = sqrt(-ab) (§39). With b = 1: sqrt(a)*sqrt(-1) = sqrt(-a), i.e. sqrt(-a) = i*sqrt(a).

(7) §59: sqrt(-ab)/sqrt(-b) = (sqrt(ab)*sqrt(-1))/(sqrt(b)*sqrt(-1)) by §58, which equals sqrt(ab)/sqrt(b) = sqrt(a) [last step implicit: cancel sqrt(-1), then sqrt(ab)/sqrt(b) = sqrt(a)]. Example: sqrt(-4)/sqrt(-2) = sqrt(2).

The catchword '§. 60.' ends the page.

Handwritten material:
- The interlinear insertion and the margin gloss are explanatory remarks on the textbook.
- The cut-off right-margin fragments (ddz/dx^2, a dy/dx^2, 'sit y=', 't=', 'aa B.', 'y=') belong to the facing manuscript page (next page).
- That next page treats d^2z/dx^2 = phi(x,y) and the Riccati equation a dy/dx = y^2 + x^n. It linearizes the Riccati equation by y = -a t'/t to a^2 t'' + x^n t = 0 and solves this by power series. None of that is worked on this page itself.
errors: §56: the statement that '-c^2 or -a^{2m} are impossible quantities' is loosely worded. -c^2 is a perfectly real (negative) number. What is meant is that it cannot be the even power (square) of a real quantity, so its square root is impossible. The handwritten insertion 'als Producte aus ihren Wurzeln betrachtet' seems intended to repair exactly this.
§56: sqrt(a^2) = ±a reflects the 18th-century two-valued reading of the radical. Under the modern principal-root convention, sqrt(a^2) = |a|.

§58 extends the real multiplication rule sqrt(x)*sqrt(y) = sqrt(xy) (§39) to the case where one factor is negative without justification. The result is correct for a,b>0 with principal roots, but the rule fails when both radicands are negative. §57 handles that case correctly by definition rather than by the rule.
No computational slips in §54 or §57–59; all identities are correct for a,b>0.

results.what: Laws of rational exponents: n-th root of a^m = a^(m/n), a^p*a^q = a^(p+q), a^p/a^q = a^(p-q), with worked examples
results.modern_name: laws of exponents for rational exponents
results.usually_credited_to: standard since Wallis/Newton (17th c.); textbook material

results.what: Even powers of real numbers are nonnegative; square roots of negative numbers are 'impossible/imaginary'
results.modern_name: nonexistence of real square roots of negatives; introduction of imaginary numbers

results.what: Elementary rules for imaginary quantities: i^2=-1, -1/i=i, sqrt(a)*sqrt(-b)=sqrt(-ab), sqrt(-ab)/sqrt(-b)=sqrt(a)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed elementary textbook page (Leiste) on rational exponents and imaginary square roots. The only handwriting is two short explanatory glosses. The Riccati/series work visible at the edge belongs to the facing page. Nothing here is Gauss's own mathematics.

checkable.asserts: the product rule sqrt(x)sqrt(y)=sqrt(xy) fails for two negative radicands (caveat to §58)

transcription_corrections: The page is a printed textbook page (Leiste), not a Gauss manuscript. Only the interlinear insertion and the margin gloss are handwritten.

The interlinear handwritten insertion 'als Producte aus ihren Wurzeln betrachtet' is written under 'gerade Potenzen sind daher', with its tail running past 'Größen.' into the margin. Its placement in the transcription is acceptable as an insertion.
The right-margin fragments (ddz/dx^2, a dy/dx^2, sit y=, t=, aa B., +, y=) are the cut-off edge of the facing manuscript page (the next page), not annotations on this page.
The machine transcription of the printed text and formulas is otherwise accurate.
